newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Many Christians said driven from homes in Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: Many Christians said driven from homes in Pakistan.

text.p: Nearly 1,000 Pakistani Christian families are living in tents after being driven from their Punjab homes by Moslem rioters, a bishop said on Wednesday.

Alexander John Malik, the Bishop of Lahore, told Reuters after visiting the Christian-populated village of Shantinagar that the whole village, including six churches, had been looted and set on fire during communal violence last Thursday.
He said about 20,000 Moslems had taken part in the attack on Shantinagar, about 100 km (62 miles) east of Multan, in Punjab province. Troops were later called in to control the unrest.
"Christians are living in tents under the supervision of army," Malik said.
"Prior to this incident, Moslems and Christians were living in a peaceful and tension-free atmosphere for many decades," he added, accusing the police of provoking the trouble.
The local deputy superintendent of police in Shantinagar was suspended after Christians accused him and two colleagues of desecrating the Bible during a raid on a Christian home.

The policemen were arrested, but released on bail. Malik said they had sought to take revenge by spreading rumours that Christians had torn pages from the Koran, written blasphemous remarks on them and thrown them into a mosque.
This sparked the riot that forced thousands of Christians to leave their homes, he added.
Two men were killed, apparently by police bullets, and 19, including a policeman, were wounded in the unrest, local officials and residents said at the time.
Most of Pakistan's 131 million people are Moslems, but there is a small Christian minority, some of whose members have been accused by radical Moslem clerics of blasphemy in recent years.
In February 1995, two Christians, one of them a 14-year-old boy, were sentenced to death for blasphemy in Lahore, but were acquitted on appeal and then emigrated to Germany.
Then-prime minister Benazir Bhutto vowed at the time to alter the blasphemy law to make it less open to abuse, but pressure from religious parties blocked any change.
